data.name: TunnelHelp_Overview
data.value: SSH tunneling (port forwarding) lets you route TCP traffic through an SSH connection. The SSH server acts as a relay: incoming connections on one side are forwarded to a target on the other side. All traffic is encrypted inside the SSH channel.

data.name: TunnelHelp_LocalDesc
data.value: Listens on your local machine at the specified address and port. When a client connects to this local port, the connection is forwarded through the SSH server to the target host and port, which must be reachable from the SSH server. Common use: access a remote database from your local tools as if it were running locally.

data.name: TunnelHelp_RemoteDesc
data.value: Opens a listening port on the SSH server. Connections to this server port are forwarded back through the SSH connection to your local machine's specified address and port. Common use: expose a local development server to the remote network or let someone on the remote side reach a service on your machine.

data.name: TunnelHelp_DynamicDesc
data.value: Creates a SOCKS5 proxy listener on your local machine. Applications configured to use this proxy will have their TCP connections routed through the SSH server, which resolves and connects to each target dynamically. Common use: browser or application traffic routing through the SSH server without configuring individual forwards.

data.name: TunnelHelp_RemoteDynamicTitle
data.value: Remote Dynamic Forward (-R without a target)

data.name: TunnelHelp_RemoteDynamicDesc
data.value: Opens a SOCKS5 proxy port on the SSH server. Remote programs that use it have this computer connect to the destinations for them — so the server can reach places only this computer can, such as an internal package mirror or API. Only destinations on the tunnel's allow list are permitted (host:port, wildcards allowed, or “any”); everything else is refused.

data.name: TunnelHelp_UnixSocketDesc
data.value: Local and remote forwards can use a Unix domain socket instead of a port. A local forward can listen on a socket file on this computer, forward to a socket on the server (such as /var/run/docker.sock), or both — so local tools work with the remote Docker or database directly and the server needs no TCP port. A remote forward has the server listen on a socket path and connects back to a socket on this computer. Socket files are protected by file permissions; the server needs AllowStreamLocalForwarding. Windows supports this from Windows 10 1803.

data.name: TunnelHelp_LoopbackNote
data.value: The meaning of 127.0.0.1 depends on which machine owns that endpoint. For a local forward's server-side target, it means the SSH server itself. For a remote forward's local service, it means this computer. On a listener endpoint, loopback restricts access to the machine hosting that listener.
